Unit 3 concepts · 3 / 60
01 · Why measuring is hard · no answer key
No right answer to check
Story so far: Unit 2 gave us stable, steerable GANs. Now: which one is actually better?
To test a network, we usually compare its output with a right answer.
classifier
guess: 7
A classifier
Every test image has a true label: “7”. Count the correct guesses: that is the accuracy.
z (noise)
G
A GAN
G (the generator) draws a brand-new 7. No true image exists to compare it with.
A new image is not right or wrong. It is only more or less like the real data.
So the score must judge all the fakes together against the real data.
Why we need a new kind of test: accuracy needs a right answer, and a GAN has none.
Unit 3 concepts · 4 / 60
01 · Why measuring is hard · two goals
Good means quality AND variety
A good GAN gets three things right at once.
Quality
Each image looks real. Sharp, clean, no odd marks.
Variety
The fakes cover all kinds in the data. Every digit, every style.
Match the real data
Each kind as common as in the real data. The fakes pass for real samples.
Trap 1: one perfect 7, again and again. Quality, no variety.
Trap 2: blurry scribbles of every kind. Variety, no quality.
Why we need both: a score that checks only one goal is fooled by the other trap.
Unit 3 concepts · 5 / 60
01 · Why measuring is hard · bad ideas
Three tempting ideas that fail
Just look
People disagree. Fifty models are too many to compare. Authors show only their best samples. A small grid can’t show a missing kind.
good GAN · bad GAN
Read D’s loss
D (the discriminator) ends up near the same loss for good and bad GANs. D being fooled may only mean D is weak.
Compare pixels
Copying the real images would win. A 7 moved slightly: almost every pixel changes.
Each idea can rank a worse GAN above a better one.
What we need: an automatic judge that sees content, not pixels, across thousands of images.
Why we need to rule these out: all three are still common, and all three can mislead.
Unit 3 concepts · 6 / 60
01 · Why measuring is hard · wish list
What a good score needs
From the failed ideas, a wish list for a GAN score:
1
Look through a trained network’s eyes
See strokes and shapes, not single pixels.
2
Judge quality AND variety
Both traps must lose.
3
Compare fakes with REAL images
The GAN’s own training data is the target.
4
One number, clear direction
Easy to say which GAN is better.
Next: the Inception Score, the first score to try. Then FID (Fréchet Inception Distance), today’s standard.
Why we need the wish list: we can hold every score up against it and see what it misses.
Unit 3 concepts · 7 / 60
02 · Inception Score · the judge
A trained classifier as judge
Story so far: Pixels and D’s loss can’t judge a GAN. Now: let a trained classifier judge.
IS (Inception Score, 2016): show the fakes to a classifier that already knows real objects.
many fakes
Inception v3
a trained image classifier
its guess for each fake
Inception v3: trained on ImageNet. About a million labelled photos, a thousand classes.
Its guess: one bar per class. Tall bar: very sure of that class.
But how can a classifier judge? A clear dog gets a confident “dog”. A muddled image confuses it.
Why we need a trained judge: it already knows what real objects look like, and it checks thousands of fakes in minutes.

02 · Inception Score · one image
One image: sure or unsure?
For one fake, Inception gives one bar per class (only four shown).
dog
cat
car
boat
Sure guess
One tall bar: “dog”. The image is sharp and clear.
dog
cat
car
boat
Unsure guess
Many low bars, all alike. The image is blurry or unclear.
A clear object matches what Inception learned from real photos. A muddle matches nothing well, so the guess spreads out.
Why we need the sure guess: it checks quality, one image at a time.

02 · Inception Score · all images
All images: same class or many?
Now add up the guesses over all the fakes: which classes appear?
dog
cat
car

Every fake: “dog”
All the guesses pile up on one class. No variety: mode collapse.
dog
cat
car
boat
Guesses spread out
Dogs, cats, cars, boats… Variety: many classes appear.
Each fake may still get a sure guess. Variety means different fakes get different sure guesses.
Why we need the total: it checks variety, which one image alone can’t show.
Unit 3 concepts · 10 / 60
02 · Inception Score · the score
The Inception Score in words
Each small chart: Inception’s guess for one fake · three fakes per case
Sure and varied
Each fake: a sure guess. Different fakes: different classes. IS high.
Sure, but all “dog”
The same guess every time. IS at its lowest.
Unsure everywhere
The same flat guess every time. IS at its lowest.
Higher is better. It rewards sure guesses that differ from fake to fake.
Compare IS only on the same dataset. A dataset with fewer classes can’t reach as high.
Why we need one number: it ranks many GANs at once, with no people involved.
Unit 3 concepts · 11 / 60
02 · Inception Score · its holes
Three holes in IS
IS (Inception Score) ticks some wishes, but not all.
real data: cats
fakes: dogs
Never looks at real images
Perfect dogs from a cat dataset. IS still scores them well.
digits?
faces?
Only knows ImageNet
No classes for digits or faces. Its guesses mean less there.
Blind inside a class
One dog, one cat, one car… Many classes, so IS looks fine. Each class has collapsed.
The biggest hole is the first: it breaks wish 3, compare fakes with real images.
Why we need something better: a GAN can score well on IS and still be wrong for its own data.

03 · FID · the idea
FID: compare fakes with real images
Story so far: IS never looks at real images. Now: compare fakes with real ones.
FID (Fréchet Inception Distance, 2017): the same Inception network, but real images go in too.
real images
Inception
features
fakes
Inception
features
compare the two sets
Inception is used for its features, not its final guess. No ImageNet classes needed.
Why we need real images in the score: only they show what the GAN was meant to learn.
Unit 3 concepts · 13 / 60
03 · FID · features
Features, not pixels
Features: what a trained network notices in an image.
early layers
edges, dots
deep layer: features read here
strokes, shapes, eyes, fur
last layer
class guess · not used
Same 7, moved a little: pixels
Almost every pixel changes. Very different.
Same 7, moved a little: features
Still a bar on top, a slanted stroke down. Almost the same.
Features say what is in an image, not exactly where.
Why we need features: they compare images by content, the way a person does.
Unit 3 concepts · 14 / 60
03 · FID · embeddings
Embeddings: an image as a feature list
An embedding: the list of numbers a trained network writes for one image.
Inception
one box per feature · dark: strongly there · pale: not there
Two 7s: close
Similar images get similar lists.
A 7 and a 3: far apart
Different shapes give different lists.
FID compares embeddings, not pixels.
Inception’s embedding is long: about two thousand numbers per image.
Why we need embeddings: they turn every image into something we can place and compare.
Unit 3 concepts · 15 / 60
03 · FID · feature space
Each image becomes a dot
Place each embedding as one dot: similar images land close. green: real images · orange: fakes
One image, one dot
Its embedding fixes where the dot sits.
Good GAN
The orange cloud sits on top of the green one.
Bad GAN
Orange cloud shifted, or the wrong shape.
Drawn flat here. The real space has one direction per feature.
But how to compare two clouds? FID checks just two things: next slide.
Why we need clouds: comparing two whole clouds checks quality and variety at once.
Unit 3 concepts · 16 / 60
03 · FID · two checks
FID checks two things
Each cloud is summed up by its centre (where it sits) and its spread (how wide, what shape). green: real images · orange: fakes
Wrong centre
Right shape, wrong place. The fakes are a different kind of image.
Wrong spread
Too narrow: too little variety. Too wide: odd extra images.
Both right
Same place, same spread. FID near zero.
FID adds the two mismatches together: the centre gap and the spread gap.
A cousin of Unit 2’s Wasserstein distance: how far apart two piles are.
Why we need both checks: a wrong centre shows poor quality; a shrunken spread shows poor variety.
Unit 3 concepts · 17 / 60
03 · FID · reading the number
Reading FID
IS (Inception Score)
FID (Fréchet Inception Distance)
looks at real images?
no
yes
checks variety?
partly
yes
better direction
higher is better
lower is better
today
rarely used
the standard
Lower is better: green end good, red end bad. The opposite of IS.
Zero: the two clouds are identical. Same centre, same spread.
FID ticks all four wishes, so papers report it first.
Why we need to read it right: a higher FID means a worse GAN, the reverse of IS.
Unit 3 concepts · 18 / 60
04 · Using FID well · the recipe
FID in five steps
Story so far: We know what FID measures. Now: how to compute it fairly.
FID (Fréchet Inception Distance) · green: real images · orange: fakes · blue: Inception v3 · purple: the measure
1 · Real
Collect many real images.
2 · Fakes
Make the same number of fakes.
3 · Features
Pass all of them through Inception.
4 · Summarise
Each cloud: its centre and spread.
5 · Compare
One number: how far apart.
Steps 1 and 2: many images, the same count on both sides.
Steps 3 and 4: the same preparation, network and summary for both.
Why we need a fixed recipe: change any step and two FID scores can no longer be compared.
Unit 3 concepts · 19 / 60
04 · Using FID well · preparation
Same preparation for both
Inception v3 (the judge network) expects big colour photos. MNIST digits are small and grey.
1 · Grey to colour
Copy the grey image into all three colour channels.
2 · Small to big
Resize it up to the size Inception expects.
3 · Same for both
Real and fake images go through exactly the same steps.
Resize real images one way and fakes another way: FID changes noticeably. That change comes from the preparation, not from G (the generator).
Why we need the same preparation: otherwise FID measures our preparation, not the GAN.
Unit 3 concepts · 20 / 60
04 · Using FID well · how many images
Too few images fool FID
high
low
true value
few images
some images
many thousands
FID of the same perfect GAN
Same perfect GAN, measured with few images: FID comes out too high.
Why: with few dots, each cloud’s centre and spread are guessed badly. Those errors show up as a mismatch.
Use many thousands of images. Always the same number for every model you compare.
Why we need many images: a small test makes a good GAN look worse than it is.
Unit 3 concepts · 21 / 60
04 · Using FID well · during training
FID while training
high
low
falling
flattening
rising
best saved copy
FID (lower is better), measured during training →
Falling: G (the generator) is learning.
Flattening: training has done what it can.
Rising: something broke, e.g. mode collapse.
Keep the checkpoint (a saved copy of G) from just before the rise.
Why we need FID during training: the losses of G and D can’t tell us when to stop; FID can.
Unit 3 concepts · 22 / 60
04 · Using FID well · a perfect score?
FID of zero is suspicious
FID (Fréchet Inception Distance) of zero: the fake cloud and the real cloud are identical. Three possible reasons:
G learned everything
New images that match the real data perfectly.
Possible, but very unlikely.
G memorised
Each fake is a copy of a training image.
Nothing new is made.
Real vs real
By mistake, both sets were real images.
A bug, not a result.
How to check: for each fake, find the most similar training image. Near-identical pairs mean G (the generator) is copying.
Why it matters: a copying GAN gets a perfect score but creates nothing new.
Unit 3 concepts · 23 / 60
04 · Using FID well · limits
What FID can’t tell you
FID (Fréchet Inception Distance) is the standard, but it has blind spots.
Simple shapes
It sums up each cloud only by its centre and its spread.
Few images
The score comes out too high and jumps around.
Fine details
Small flaws barely change the features, so FID misses them.
Inception’s eyes
Its features come from photos. Less meaningful for digits or X-rays.
No reason given
It says that images are bad, not why.
So in practice
Always look at sample images too. Add other measures (next section).
Why it matters: knowing the blind spots tells us what else to check.

05 · Beyond one number · the problem
Two GANs, same FID
Story so far: FID gives one number. Now: what one number hides.
Two GANs trained on the same handwritten digits, 0 to 9.
01234
56789
GAN A
Draws all ten digits. But every digit is blurry.
01234
56789
GAN B
Every digit is sharp. But it draws only six digits.
A · B
Same FID
FID (Fréchet Inception Distance) scores them about the same.
FID adds every kind of mismatch into one number. Blur and missing digits can add up to the same total.
Why we need more than FID: to fix a GAN we must know whether it lacks quality or variety.
Unit 3 concepts · 25 / 60
05 · Beyond one number · two scores
Precision and recall
green cloud: real images · orange dots: fakes · all as dots in Inception’s feature space, as for FID
Precision: quality
Of all the fakes, how many land inside the real cloud? Crossed dots: fakes that look like no real image.
Recall: variety
How much of the real cloud do the fakes cover? Grey half: real kinds G (the generator) never makes.
Each is a share, from none to all. Higher is better for both.
Two separate scores: quality and variety are no longer mixed.
Why we need two scores: they say which of quality or variety is missing.
Unit 3 concepts · 26 / 60
05 · Beyond one number · reading both
Reading the two together
green: real cloud · orange: fakes
Both high: great
Fakes look real and cover every kind.
High precision, low recall
Sharp, few kinds: mode collapse. GAN B is here.
Low precision, high recall
All kinds, but many look wrong: blurry. GAN A is here.
Both low: poor
Fakes look wrong and miss most kinds.
GAN A and GAN B had the same FID. Precision and recall tell them apart at once.
Why it matters: each corner calls for a different fix.

Unit 3 concepts · 28 / 60
06 · Strengths and weaknesses · strengths
What GANs do well
Story so far: We can now score a GAN. Now: where do GANs win and lose?
Sharp images
D (the discriminator) punishes blur.
Fast
One pass through G (the generator) per image.
Smooth latent space
Walk and steer z (the noise vector), Unit 2.
Plugs in anywhere
Add a D to other models (Units 4 and 5).
Why sharp: a blurry image is easy for D to call fake. So G is pushed towards crisp detail, not a safe blurry average.
Why we need this list: it tells us when a GAN is the right tool.
Unit 3 concepts · 29 / 60
06 · Strengths and weaknesses · weaknesses
Where GANs struggle
Five weaknesses of GANs (generative adversarial networks):
Unstable training
G (generator) and D (discriminator) can swing instead of settling.
Mode collapse
G covers only some kinds of image.
No likelihood
It can make an image, but can’t say how likely any given image is.
Hard to evaluate
No right answer to check: this whole unit.
No way back
No built-in way to find the z (the noise vector) behind a real image.
What is left
Units 2 and 3 eased the first, second and fourth. The third and fifth remain.
Why we need this list: it tells us when another kind of generator may be the better choice.
Unit 3 concepts · 30 / 60
06 · Strengths and weaknesses · other generators
Other ways to generate images
VAE
variational autoencoder
Squeeze an image into a short code, then rebuild it.
✓ stable to train
✗ often blurry
Autoregressive
one piece after another
Draw one pixel at a time, each based on the ones before.
✓ good variety
✗ very slow
Flow model
reversible steps
A chain of steps that can run backwards too.
✓ exact likelihood
✗ heavy, costly
Diffusion
remove noise slowly
Start from pure noise, remove a little noise many times.
✓ sharp and varied
✗ slow: many steps
A GAN (generative adversarial network) makes an image in one pass: no chain of steps. But its training is less stable, and it can’t say how likely an image is.
Why we need to know them: the right generator depends on what matters most: speed, sharpness, stability or likelihood.

Each family gets about two of three wishes: quality, variety, speed.

Unit 3 concepts · 32 / 60
07 · Bias and fairness · what is bias
A good score can still be unfair
Story so far: We can measure a GAN. Now: what if a ‘good’ GAN learned the wrong things?
Bias: the GAN’s images don’t fairly represent the variety of people. Sometimes not even the variety in its own training data.
Skin tone
Mostly light-skinned faces. Darker faces rare and less detailed.
young
old
Age
Mostly young faces. Older faces rare and blurry.
7
7
7
7
7
Digit style
Upright 7s everywhere. The slanted style never appears.
FID (Fréchet Inception Distance) can still look great. The majority’s images are good, and they dominate the score.
Why we need to look for bias: GAN images are used to train other systems that affect people.
Unit 3 concepts · 33 / 60
07 · Bias and fairness · three levels
Three places bias enters
blue: group A (many images) · teal: group B (few images)
1 · The data
Unbalanced to begin with: many A, few B.
2 · The model
The GAN makes the gap worse: even more A, even fewer B.
3 · The evaluation
One overall score looks fine. B’s poor images are averaged away.
Each level hands its problem to the next: unbalanced data, a model that widens the gap, a score that hides it.
Why we need three levels: each level needs its own check and its own fix.
Unit 3 concepts · 34 / 60
07 · Bias and fairness · where bias comes from
Many places bias comes from
Bias in machine learning can enter at every step, not only in the data.
1 · Collecting data
Who gets photographed, and where.
2 · Labelling
Who decides the labels, and how.
3 · History
The past was already unfair; data records it.
4 · Measuring
A poor stand-in for what we care about.
8 · Feedback
Its outputs become tomorrow’s data.
7 · Using it
Applied to people it never saw.
6 · Evaluating
One average score hides weak groups.
5 · The model
It learns the majority best.
Step 8 closes the loop: GAN images are often reused as training data, so today’s bias feeds step 1.
Why we need the whole map: fixing one step can’t remove bias that enters at another.

07 · Bias and fairness · amplification
GANs make imbalance worse
training data
group A
B

group A

Group B’s share shrinks: the GAN does not just copy the imbalance.
why: a loop
more A examples
more feedback for A

G gets better at A
Feedback: the corrections G (the generator) gets from D (the discriminator). Few B images: little feedback for B, so G stays worse at B and draws it less.
Why we need to watch the output balance: the loop turns a small imbalance into a bigger one.

07 · Bias and fairness · mode collapse
Mode collapse hits minorities first
Each green cluster: one kind of image · big cluster: a common kind · small cluster: a rare kind
Before: many kinds
Common kinds and rare kinds, all in the real data.
After collapse
Kinds disappear. The rare ones vanish first.
1
0
7
8
9
4
Digits too
Easy, common shapes survive. Harder ones drop out.
Not random: which kinds vanish follows the data’s structure. Rare kinds get the least feedback, so they go first.
Why it matters: mode collapse is a fairness problem, not just a technical one.
Unit 3 concepts · 37 / 60
07 · Bias and fairness · real harms
Real harms
A biased GAN’s images rarely stay on screen: they become input for other systems.
Synthetic training data
A face detector trained on GAN faces
works worse on under-represented faces
Medical images
Synthetic X-rays learned from one hospital’s patients
a model that works worse for other populations
Art tools
A generator trained mostly on Western art
other styles poorly shown or stereotyped
Deepfake detection
Detectors trained on biased fakes
miss fakes of minority groups more often
Same pattern each time: the GAN’s bias is passed on to a system that affects people.
Why it matters: biased images shape real decisions about real people.
Unit 3 concepts · 38 / 60
07 · Bias and fairness · finding bias
How to find bias in a GAN
blue, teal, brown: three groups, e.g. age groups or digit classes
1 · Count the data
How many training images does each group have?
2 · Score each group
FID (Fréchet Inception Distance) for each group on its own. Same number of images per group.
3 · Look at each group
A grid of images per group. Blurrier, less varied, odd details?
But how do we get fakes of one group? Use a cGAN (conditional GAN): ask for that group’s label.
Why the same number? Fewer images push FID up, so a small group would look worse unfairly.
Why we need these steps: bias we don’t measure stays hidden.
Unit 3 concepts · 39 / 60
07 · Bias and fairness · per-group scores
One score can hide a group
bad
good
overall
group A
group B
group C
FID (Fréchet Inception Distance): lower is better
Overall FID: looks great.
Split by group: A and B fine, C terrible.
Many good A and B images average away C’s bad ones.
Report a score per group, with the same number of images each.
Why we need per-group scores: an average can’t show who is left behind.
Unit 3 concepts · 40 / 60
07 · Bias and fairness · fixes
Five ways to reduce bias
1 · Balance the data
Repeat rare examples, or use fewer common ones.
Repeating can overfit; dropping wastes data.
2 · cGAN with group labels
A cGAN (conditional GAN) gives each group its own signal.
G (the generator) can make every group; quality gaps may remain.
3 · Weight the loss
Mistakes on rare groups count more.
D (the discriminator) pays more attention, so G gets a stronger push.
4 · Check per group
Per-group scores and image grids, every time.
Finds the problem; does not fix it alone.
5 · Collect better data
Data that represents everyone it will be used on.
The best fix: prevention.
Remember
No algorithm can fully fix badly biased data.
Why we need several fixes: bias enters at several places, so one fix is never enough.
Unit 3 concepts · 41 / 60
07 · Bias and fairness · the tension
Fair can mean a worse FID
blue: group A · teal: group B · bar: share of images
The real data
Unbalanced: mostly group A.
A copying GAN
Copies the imbalance. FID (Fréchet Inception Distance): low.
A fair GAN
Rebalanced: both groups equal. FID: higher.
FID rewards matching the data, imbalance included. The fair GAN no longer matches the unbalanced data, so its FID gets worse.
That is acceptable: a feature, not a bug.
Why it matters: the best number is not always the best GAN.
Unit 3 concepts · 42 / 60
07 · Bias and fairness · checklist
Before you deploy a GAN
The data and the model
Which groups exist in my data?
How balanced are they?
Have I computed per-group scores?
Are some groups blurrier or less varied?
The use and the people
What will this GAN be used for?
Who could be harmed by biased output?
Have I documented the known limits?
Have I tried the fixes?
Answer all eight before the GAN’s images reach anyone.
Why it matters: bias is far cheaper to catch before deployment than after harm is done.
Unit 3 concepts · 43 / 60
08 · StyleGAN · the problem
One z controls everything
Story so far: We can measure and audit GANs. Now: the generator that made faces photo-real.
DCGAN (deep convolutional GAN, Unit 1): z (the noise vector) goes in once, at the very start.
z → layers → face
1 · z enters once
Only the first layer sees z. Later layers only see the layer before.
one number of z changed
2 · Nudge one number
Hair, face shape and background all change together.
one number → many features
3 · Tangled (Unit 2)
No single number means just “hair”.
StyleGAN (Karras et al., 2019): photo-real faces, with separate controls for shape and detail.
Its new ideas all sit inside G (the generator): how and where the noise reaches the layers.
Why we need StyleGAN: to change one feature of a face without changing everything else.

z space
2 · z: a fixed round shape
z must fill a round, even shape. Features get squeezed and bent to fit.
w space
3 · w: any shape it needs
w can take the data’s own shape. Features can sit apart.
But who teaches w its shape? Nobody labels features: the mapping network learns only from D’s (the discriminator’s) feedback, with G.
Result: moving w changes fewer features at once than moving z.
Why we need the mapping network: it gives the layers a style code whose features are less tangled.

08 · StyleGAN · idea 2
Idea 2: wipe the style, paint a new one
Inside a layer the image is a stack of channels: one map per pattern the layer finds (here: three, each with one stroke).
three channels before
1 · The old style
Each channel has its own strength and brightness: dark, pale, medium.
instance normalisation
2 · Wash it out
Make every channel plain and even. The stroke stays, the old look goes.
new style from w
3 · Paint the new style
w decides how strong and how bright each channel becomes.
AdaIN (adaptive instance normalisation): wash out, then repaint from w.
Why wash first? The old style can’t leak through: only w sets the look.
Why we need AdaIN: it is how w actually steers what each layer draws.

w enters every layer
w
style code
layer
small

layer

the same w goes to every layer
blue: each layer’s own reader
The same w goes to every layer, smallest to largest.
Each layer’s own reader takes only what it needs from w.
DCGAN (deep convolutional GAN): z enters once. StyleGAN: style at every layer.
Why we need it: every size of detail, from shape to texture, is steered directly by w.

08 · StyleGAN · what each layer controls
Coarse, medium, fine
Change the style in one group of layers only, and watch what changes in the face.
early, small layers
Coarse
Face shape, pose, head angle.
middle layers
Medium
Eyes, nose, mouth.
late, large layers
Fine
Skin texture, freckles, hair strands, colour.
A small layer has only a few pixels: room for the overall shape only. Large layers have room for the tiniest details.
How do we know? Give different layers different w’s: style mixing, next.
Why we need this split: we can edit shape, features or texture separately.
Unit 3 concepts · 49 / 60
08 · StyleGAN · style mixing
Style mixing
Give the layers two different w’s: one for the early layers, one for the later layers.
round face, head tilted
Face A
Its w goes to the early, small layers.
long face, red hair, freckles
Face B
Its w goes to the later, large layers.
round, tilted, red hair, freckles
Mixed face
A’s face shape and pose, B’s colouring and texture.
Impossible in DCGAN (deep convolutional GAN): z enters once, so shape and colour can’t be split.
Also used during training: random mixing keeps each layer’s style independent.
Why we need style mixing: it proves each layer’s style is separate.

08 · StyleGAN · idea 3
Idea 3: noise for random detail
A little fresh random noise is added inside every layer, new for every image.
curls in one place
Same w, noise 1
Curly hair.
curls moved
Same w, noise 2
Same person, same curls, each curl in a new spot.
a new style
New w
A different person: straight, fair hair.
Style (w) decides what: “this person has curly hair”.
Noise decides exactly where each curl, hair and pore falls.
Why we need noise: real faces have tiny random details that belong to no one’s style.

08 · StyleGAN · idea 4
Idea 4: start from a learned block
Where do the layers begin? yellow: z (the noise vector) · green: learned block · purple: w
z → block → layers
DCGAN
z is reshaped into the first small block. Every image starts from its own z.
block → layers, w and noise join in
StyleGAN
The same learned block for every image. Training adjusts it like any weight.
new w and noise → new faces
Then where is the variety?
Only in w and the noise.
z never touches the layers directly: it reaches them only through w.
Why is that enough? Every layer already gets its look from w.
Why we need it: each input has one clear job: w sets the style, noise adds detail.
Unit 3 concepts · 52 / 60
08 · StyleGAN · training trick
Grow the image step by step
The first StyleGAN trained G and D (the discriminator) on small images first.
very small
1 · Start tiny
Train on very small images: only rough shape and colour.
bigger, new layer fading in
2 · Add layers
Add layers for a bigger size. Fade each new layer in slowly.
full size
3 · Full size
Each step only adds detail.
Fading in: at first the image comes mostly from the old, trained layers. The new layer’s share grows until it takes over.
Borrowed from ProGAN (progressive GAN, Karras et al., 2018). StyleGAN 2 dropped it for a better design.
Why we need growing: a huge image is very unstable to learn in one go; small first is easy.
Unit 3 concepts · 53 / 60
08 · StyleGAN · truncation
Truncation in style space
Unit 2: keep z (the noise vector) near the centre to trade variety for quality · dots: w’s · green star: the average w
many w’s
1 · The average w
Map many random z’s to w. Their average gives the “average face”.
far w’s pulled in
2 · Pull w closer
Closer to the average: cleaner, more ordinary faces.
far w’s kept
3 · Leave w far out
More variety, but some odd faces.
A dial: from “always the average face” to “full variety”.
Smoother than in z: w is less tangled, so every style shrinks evenly to the average.
Why we need it: we choose our balance of quality and variety, with cleaner results than in z.

08 · StyleGAN · three versions
StyleGAN 1, 2, 3
2019
StyleGAN 1
The ideas you just saw, including the growing step.
2020
StyleGAN 2
No more blobs (“water droplets”). No growing step. Smoother walks through w.
2021 · faded face: before the move
StyleGAN 3
Fixed “texture sticking”: details stuck to the screen as the face moved.
StyleGAN 2 applies the style in a cleaner way than AdaIN (adaptive instance normalisation).
Every version keeps the core: a mapping network and style at every layer.
Why it matters: each version fixed a visible flaw but kept the core ideas.

08 · StyleGAN · why it matters
Why StyleGAN matters
w into every layer
Ideas everywhere
Mapping networks and style at every layer are now common.
photo → w → edited photo
GAN inversion
Find the w for a real photo, then edit it.
same design, new data
Beyond faces
Trained on cars, rooms, cats and art.
It proved that GANs can be photo-real. That pushed the whole field forward.
A face StyleGAN can even be adjusted to draw cartoon faces.
Why it matters: StyleGAN’s ideas, not just its faces, shaped the generators that followed.

Unit 3 concepts · 57 / 60
09 · Wrap-up · ten ideas
Ten ideas to remember
Measure (sections 01–05)
1
Judge with a trained network: Inception’s features, not pixels.
2
IS (Inception Score): sure guesses and varied guesses.
3
Embeddings: each image becomes a list of features; FID (Fréchet Inception Distance) compares the real and fake clouds.
4
Fair comparisons: lower FID is better; same preparation, many images, same count.
5
No perfect measure: each has a weak spot, so pair FID with precision and recall.
Choose, be fair, build (06–08)
6
Other generators: VAEs (variational autoencoders) stable but blurry; diffusion sharp but slow; GANs sharp and fast but unstable.
7
Bias comes from everywhere: data, labels, history, model, evaluation, use.
8
Detect it: count each group, score each group, look at each group; GANs make imbalance worse.
9
Mapping network: z (the noise vector) becomes w (a style code).
10
Style at every layer: coarse to fine; noise adds random detail.
Why we need these ten: every GAN in Units 4 and 5 will be judged, checked and built with them.
Unit 3 concepts · 58 / 60
09 · Wrap-up · quiz
Explain in one sentence
1 · Why can’t IS (Inception Score) catch perfect dogs drawn from a cat dataset?
IS never looks at the real images.
2 · Why does FID compare embeddings, not pixels?
A slightly shifted image changes every pixel, but hardly changes its features.
3 · Why is an FID of zero suspicious?
G may have copied the training images, or real was compared with real.
4 · Why can one FID hide an unfair GAN?
A great average can cover one group with terrible images.
5 · When would you choose diffusion over a GAN?
When quality and variety matter more than speed.
6 · What does style mixing show?
Each layer’s style is separate: shape from one face, colour from another.
Why it matters: if you can say each answer in one sentence, you understand Unit 3.

Image-to-image
An image in, an image out. For example, a sketch in, a photo out.
Pix2Pix

Why it follows: we can now build, measure and audit a GAN. Next: put GANs to work on real images.
